title: 07. Messaging & Event-Driven Architecture: Apache Pulsar
summary: Apache Pulsar is a distributed pub-sub messaging and streaming platform that separates the stateless compute layer (brokers) from the durable storage layer (Apache BookKeeper bookies), supports flexible subscription modes…
objectives: Why does Pulsar separate brokers and bookies, and what does this buy operationally?
What are Pulsar's four subscription modes, and when would you pick each?
How does Pulsar's geo-replication differ from Kafka's MirrorMaker 2?
What is a BookKeeper ledger, and how does the quorum model work?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Apache Pulsar is a distributed pub-sub messaging and streaming platform that separates the stateless compute layer (brokers) from the durable storage layer (Apache BookKeeper bookies), supports flexible subscription modes (exclusive, shared, failover, key_shared) on top of a partitioned-topic log, and offers built-in geo-replication and tiered storage for global, multi-tenant workloads.

Apache Pulsar was originally developed at Yahoo in 2013 to address limitations they hit running Kafka at scale — rigid broker coupling, painful rebalances, and difficult geo-replication across datacenters. Yahoo open-sourced Pulsar in 2016, and it became a top-level Apache project in 2018. The defining architectural decision is the **separation of compute from storage**: brokers are stateless serving nodes that handle producers, consumers, topic ownership, and routing, while bookies (Apache BookKeeper nodes) store the actual message ledgers durably as replicated quorum writes. This split — pioneered in Pulsar and later echoed in systems like Uber's JetStream and Redpanda's tiered modes — gives Pulsar properties that Kafka's coupled brokers cannot match: instant broker failover (a dead broker's topics are re-assigned in seconds because no data lives on the broker), independent scaling of read/write throughput vs. storage capacity, and the ability to add bookies without rebalancing petabytes of historical data across brokers. Tencent runs Pulsar at petabyte scale for its IM, gaming, and payment pipelines; Splunk uses it as the ingestion backbone; Yahoo Japan still operates it for real-time notification fan-out; Twitter adopted it for parts of its event pipeline after hitting Kafka rebalance pain.

The data model is **topics, partitions, and subscriptions**. A topic is a named log stream (`persistent://tenant/namespace/topic`), and like Kafka it can be partitioned (typically 1 to 100s of partitions) for parallelism. Producers write messages with optional keys (keys route to a partition deterministically, preserving per-key ordering) and can choose sync vs. async send, batching, and compression. Messages are appended to a **ledger** per partition — a BookKeeper abstraction that is a write-once, sealed-on-close sequence of entries replicated across N bookies (default ensemble=3, write-quorum=3, ack-quorum=2 — meaning writes are acked after 2 of 3 bookies confirm, balancing latency and durability). When a ledger fills or a broker fails, a new ledger is started; old ledgers are sealed and remain readable. The ledger abstraction is what makes broker failover instant: a new broker simply opens a new ledger on the same bookies, and historical data stays where it is. Contrast with Kafka, where a broker failure means electing a new partition leader from in-sync replicas and possibly replaying unflushed data.

Pulsar's **subscription model** is richer than Kafka's consumer-group abstraction and is one of Pulsar's strongest differentiators. Four subscription modes cover almost every messaging pattern: **Exclusive** (one consumer per subscription — like a point-to-point queue), **Shared** (round-robin delivery across N consumers with per-message ack, like SQS or RabbitMQ work queues), **Failover** (one active consumer, others stand by as hot backups, ordered takeover), and **Key_Shared** (messages with the same key always go to the same consumer, even across rebalances — solving Kafka's "key ordering lost on rebalance" pain). Multiple independent subscriptions can attach to the same topic, and each tracks its own cursor (position in the log), so one subscription can be live (seconds behind) while another replays from hour-old data — Kafka-style consumer-group fan-out is fully supported, but with the added flexibility of per-subscription semantics. This means a single Pulsar topic can simultaneously serve a streaming consumer (shared subscription, parallel processing), a key-ordered consumer (key_shared for per-user ordering), and a replay consumer (exclusive subscription reading from earliest offset) — all without code changes on the producer side.

**Geo-replication** is built into Pulsar's DNA via the namespace config, not bolted on as a connector. A namespace can be configured to replicate to other Pulsar clusters (e.g., `us-east`, `us-west`, `eu-west`), and producers write locally while Pulsar internally replicates messages to remote clusters over dedicated replication links with their own backlog and retry semantics. Consumers in each region read locally with low latency, and the system tolerates region failures gracefully — cross-region lag is typically sub-second to seconds, depending on network distance. This is significantly simpler than Kafka's MirrorMaker 2, which runs as a separate process and struggles with offset translation and exactly-once across clusters. Companies like Yahoo Japan and Tencent rely on Pulsar's native geo-replication for multi-region active-active deployments. **Tiered storage** extends Pulsar's reach for long-retention workloads: when a topic's data ages past a threshold (e.g., 1 hour), BookKeeper ledgers are offloaded to object storage (S3, Azure Blob, GCS) while remaining transparently readable via brokers — so you can keep a year of telemetry data without provisioning bookie capacity for it, paying object-storage prices for cold data. Kafka added Tiered Storage only recently (KIP-405) and it is far less mature.

The **trade-offs** vs. Kafka are real and worth being precise about. Pulsar's wins: instant broker failover (no leader election, no ISR wait), independent compute/storage scaling, four subscription modes (vs. Kafka's one), native geo-replication, tiered storage, and multi-tenancy built into the URL (`tenant/namespace/topic`). Pulsar's losses: a smaller ecosystem than Kafka (fewer connectors, fewer streams-processing libraries with first-class support, less community knowledge in the job market), higher operational complexity (two distributed systems to run — brokers and bookies — plus ZooKeeper), and at the high end of single-partition throughput Pulsar has historically lagged Kafka slightly due to BookKeeper's quorum write overhead (each message touches 3 bookies vs. Kafka's single-leader write). Pulsar is the right call when you need flexible subscription semantics, true multi-tenancy across teams, geo-replication across regions, or elastic scaling of storage and compute independently — common in large multi-product organizations. Kafka remains the better default for greenfield high-throughput streaming where the team already knows Kafka and the ecosystem matters. The architect's rule: Pulsar for flexible, multi-tenant, geo-distributed messaging; Kafka for raw streaming throughput with a mature ecosystem; RabbitMQ for rich routing and per-message control at lower throughput.

key=user_99] end B1 -->|round-robin| C1 B1 --> C2 B2 --> C3 B1 -->|sticky by key| KC1 B2 -->|sticky by key| KC2 ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +------+ produce("orders", key, msg) +--------------------------+ | Prod |------------------------------------>| Stateless Broker Layer | +------+ | (no data on disk) | +---+------------------+---+ | | owns partition-0 | owns partition-1| v v quorum write (E=3, W=3, A=2) | | +---------------------------------------+ | | | | | v v v v +-------+ +-------+ +-------+ +-------+ |Bookie | |Bookie | |Bookie | |Bookie | | 1 | | 2 | | 2 | | 3 | | L0-0 | | L0-0 | | L1-0 | | L1-0 | | L0-1 | | L0-1 | | L1-1 | | L1-1 | +---+---+ +---+---+ +---+---+ +---+---+ | | | | +------ ack ---+ +------ ack ---+ (2 of 3 ack = success) broker failure: new broker opens new ledger, old ledgers stay on bookies --> no data migration, failover in seconds Subscriptions on same topic: +-----------------------------------------------------------+ | Topic: persistent://tenant/prod/orders (partitioned x2) | +-----+-----------------+----------------+------------------+ | | | v v v +-------------+ +---------------+ +------------------+ | shared (3) | | key_shared(2) | | failover (1+1) | | round-robin | | sticky-by-key | | active + standby | +-------------+ +---------------+ +------------------+ (each tracks its own cursor in ZooKeeper) ``` ### Walkthrough 1. **Producers contact brokers** (stateless). The broker that owns partition-0 of `orders` accepts the write, assigns a sequence ID, and prepares a ledger entry. The producer sees a single endpoint; the broker handles partition routing and key hashing. 2. **Broker writes to bookies in quorum.** The entry is sent to 3 bookies (ensemble=3, write-quorum=3); once 2 acknowledge (ack-quorum=2), the broker acks the producer. The data is now durably replicated — even if the broker dies immediately, the entry survives on bookies. 3. **Consumers attach subscriptions.** A `shared` subscription fans messages round-robin across 3 consumers with per-message ack; a `key_shared` subscription pins each key to one consumer so per-key order holds across rebalances. Each subscription's cursor (last-acked message ID) is persisted in ZooKeeper, so consumer restarts resume exactly where they left off. 4. **On broker failure**, ZooKeeper detects it within seconds; ownership of partition-0 moves to another broker, which opens a fresh ledger on the same bookies. Historical ledgers remain readable on the original bookies — no data migration, no leader election stall. 5. **Tiered storage offloads cold ledgers** to S3 when they age past the threshold, while brokers continue serving reads transparently. Geo-replication asynchronously mirrors messages to remote Pulsar clusters via built-in replication links, giving active-active multi-region consumption.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
"""Apache Pulsar-style broker mock: separated broker (compute) + bookie
(storage) layers, with the four subscription modes. Run: python pulsar_mock.py"""
import hashlib
from collections import defaultdict
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Message:  # a single produced record
    msg_id: int; key: str; value: str

class Bookie:  # storage node; holds ledgers
    def __init__(self, name): self.name, self.ledgers = name, defaultdict(list)
    def write(self, ledger_id, msg): self.ledgers[ledger_id].append(msg)

class BookKeeper:  # quorum writer across N bookies (E, W, A)
    def __init__(self, bookies, write_q=3, ack_q=2):
        self.bookies, self.W, self.A = bookies, write_q, ack_q
    def write(self, ledger_id, msg):
        acks = 0
        for b in self.bookies[:self.W]:      # send to W bookies
            b.write(ledger_id, msg); acks += 1
            if acks >= self.A: break         # ack-quorum reached -> durable
        return True

class Broker:  # stateless compute; owns partitions, routes, serves consumers
    def __init__(self, bk): self.bk = bk; self.next_id = 0
    def produce(self, topic, key, value):
        part = int(hashlib.md5(key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % 2  # 2 partitions
        msg = Message(self.next_id, key, value); self.next_id += 1
        self.bk.write(f"{topic}-p{part}", msg)  # durable on bookies, not broker
        return msg

class Subscription:  # four modes: exclusive, shared, failover, key_shared
    def __init__(self, name, mode):
        self.name, self.mode = name, mode
        self.cursor = 0; self.consumers = []; self.key_owner = {}
    def register(self, cid):
        if self.mode == "exclusive" and self.consumers:
            raise RuntimeError("exclusive: only 1 consumer allowed")
        self.consumers.append(cid)
    def deliver(self, msg):
        if self.mode == "shared":
            c = self.consumers[self.cursor % len(self.consumers)]      # round-robin
        elif self.mode == "failover":
            c = self.consumers[0]                                      # active; rest standby
        elif self.mode == "key_shared":
            if msg.key not in self.key_owner:                          # sticky by key
                self.key_owner[msg.key] = self.consumers[len(self.key_owner) % len(self.consumers)]
            c = self.key_owner[msg.key]
        else:  # exclusive
            c = self.consumers[0]
        self.cursor += 1
        return f"[{self.name}/{self.mode}] {c} <- id={msg.msg_id} key={msg.key}"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    bk = BookKeeper([Bookie(f"bk{i}") for i in range(3)])
    broker = Broker(bk)
    sub_sh = Subscription("billing", "shared");    [sub_sh.register(c) for c in ("c1","c2","c3")]
    sub_ks = Subscription("enrich", "key_shared"); [sub_ks.register(c) for c in ("ca","cb")]
    for i, k in enumerate(["user_42","user_99","user_42","user_7","user_99"]):
        m = broker.produce("orders", k, f"order-{i}")
        print(sub_sh.deliver(m)); print(sub_ks.deliver(m))
# Sample output shows shared round-robin + key_shared sticky-by-key.
```

quiz.explanation: Pulsar's separation of stateless brokers (compute) from BookKeeper bookies (storage) means a broker holds no data on disk — it only owns a partition temporarily and writes entries to a quorum of bookies. The operational payoff appears during failure: when a broker dies, ZooKeeper detects it within seconds and reassigns its partitions to a surviving broker, which simply opens a new ledger on the same bookies.
